summary: Describes private SIP extensions between proxies that support the PacketCable Distributed Call Signaling architecture. Telephone service providers need to exchange trusted information about customers and calls when operating across domains, and these extensions provide that.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds five private fields to SIP, the protocol used to set up phone calls. The fields carry customer and billing details, trace requests for harassing calls, operator service requests and lawful surveillance instructions between the trusted parts of a cable provider's network. They are only used inside a closed group of providers that trust each other, and they are removed before any message leaves that group.

questions: how do sip proxies exchange trusted caller information
what is a private-url in packetcable sip
how does p-dcs-osps request a busy line check
subtitle: Private SIP header fields that let cable providers swap billing, tracing and surveillance data inside their own networks.

tldr.problem: A residential telephone service that spans several providers needs the trusted elements in each domain to exchange trusted information about the call and the customers on it: who is calling, how to charge for the call, and what a trace or lawful surveillance order requires.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five private SIP header fields. Each is inserted when a request enters a trusted network segment and removed before it leaves, and the RFC states exactly which user agents and proxies may add, replace, check or pass each one.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3603. It applies only inside closed administrative domains or federations that have agreed policies, because the headers carry customer data that must not leave the provider's control.

facts.label: Billing-Correlation-ID structure
facts.value: 24 bytes: 4 bytes of NTP timestamp, 8 bytes of element identifier, 8 bytes of time zone, 4 bytes of sequence number

facts.label: Financial-Entity-ID encoding
facts.value: Up to 16 hexadecimal characters, followed by @ and the host

today: RFC 5503 was published in March 2009 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 3603, which it updates with a timestamp parameter on the trace header, a jurisdiction parameter on the billing header and correlation identifiers on the surveillance header. The document has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Where the Extensions May Be Used
sections.content:
The extensions described here assume a particular network topology, a known link between SIP and the layers below it, and a transitive trust relationship between the parties. The RFC says plainly that these assumptions are generally not applicable in the Internet as a whole.

The headers are therefore only used within closed administrative domains, or among federations of administrative domains that have already agreed policies for coordinating charging and other functions, as in the PacketCable Distributed Call Signaling architecture. Use outside such a domain could result in the leakage of potentially sensitive or private information. The RFC also urges operators to obtain user consent to the privacy implications of those policies.

The document uses the requirement keywords of RFC 2119, but the scope of that language is limited to the area of applicability just described. The technology, the RFC notes, does not apply to the general Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: These headers are meant for a closed group of providers that trust each other, such as one cable network. Putting them on the open Internet could leak customer billing and call data, so the RFC limits them to domains that have agreed policies in advance.

sections.title: Why These Extensions Exist
sections.content:
Deploying a residential telephone service based on SIP at a very large scale across different domains requires trusted elements owned by different service providers to exchange trusted information about the parties in a call and about the customer behind them.

The Distributed Call Signaling architecture separates call signalling from resource management. Proxies act as policy decision points and trusted intermediaries along the signalling path. Edge routers provide the network connectivity and enforce resource policy, and they capture and report network connectivity and resource usage. Those edge routers need billing information they can log with Record-Keeping or billing servers. The proxy can supply it, because the proxy acts as the central point of coordination between call signalling and resource management and knows the authenticated identity of the calling and called parties. Since there is a trust relationship among the proxies, they can be relied upon to exchange trusted billing information about the parties in a call.

The RFC lists the services that need this. They are access network coordination to prevent theft of service, customer originated trace of harassing calls, operator services such as busy line verification, emergency services such as 9-1-1 calls to a Public Service Access Point, and electronic surveillance and law enforcement access as required by legislation and court orders.

Two details shape the design. The SIP Call-ID header cannot serve as the identifier for usage accounting records, because the originating user agent chooses it and it need not be unique across past and current calls. And billing information is neither unique to a user nor identical for every call from that user, so it has to travel in its own header rather than be derived from the party identification.
sections.plainLanguage: Different providers each run part of the phone network, so they need a trusted way to swap customer and billing details about a call. The RFC adds private fields to SIP for that, along with fields for tracing harassing calls, for operator services and for lawful surveillance.

sections.title: The Trust Boundary
sections.content:
The Distributed Call Signaling architecture defines a trust boundary around the systems and servers that the service provider owns, operates or controls. Inside the boundary sit the proxies and servers such as bridge servers, voicemail servers and announcement servers. Outside the boundary lie customer premises equipment and various application and media servers operated by third-party service providers.

Some subscriber-specific information stays inside the boundary. Billing and accounting information stays there. Other subscriber information, such as endpoint identity, may be presented to untrusted endpoints or may be withheld based on subscriber profiles.

A user agent may be inside the trust boundary or outside it, depending on exactly what function it is performing and how. The procedures therefore differ for trusted and untrusted user agents. Because a user agent can support both client and server functions, the rules are further split into user agent client and user agent server cases, and each of the five header sections repeats that split.

The RFC also defines a private-URL: a SIP URI generated by a proxy whose host and port identify the proxy and whose user information part holds data the proxy does not want disclosed outside its trusted domain, such as billing account numbers, surveillance indications and call redirection information. The data is either stored locally by the proxy or encrypted with a private key known only to that proxy, and a checksum in the user information detects tampering. The mechanism a proxy uses to recognise and decode such a URL is local to the proxy and is not standardised.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC draws a line around everything the provider controls: its proxies, voicemail and announcement servers. Customer equipment and third-party servers sit outside that line. Billing data never crosses it, and the rules for a user agent depend on whether it sits inside or outside.

sections.title: The Five Private Header Fields
sections.content:
The RFC adds five header fields to the SIP header registry, and describes each with ABNF, the syntax notation defined in RFC 5234.

P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID supports the customer originated trace service, where a called party can report an obscene or harassing call to law enforcement. The service is independent of caller identity and works even when the caller asked for anonymity, but the called party must be able to trust that the calling identity presented is valid. The header appears only in an INVITE request. Its syntax is P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID = "P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID" HCOLON name-addr *1(SEMI timestamp-param) *(SEMI trace-param), where the timestamp parameter holds the time the user agent received the session initiation request, in the Network Time Protocol timestamp format of RFC 1305, encoded in UTF-8, and the trace parameter is a generic parameter reserved for future extensions.

P-DCS-OSPS tells a user agent that a call needs special handling that ordinary call processing would not give, such as a busy line check by a telephone operator. Its syntax is P-DCS-OSPS = "P-DCS-OSPS" HCOLON OSPS-Tag, with OSPS-Tag = "BLV" / "EI" / "RING" / token. The three defined values are busy line verification, emergency interrupt and operator ringback; the last alternative, token, is reserved for future use.

P-DCS-Billing-Info carries the accounting data for a call. It starts with a Billing-Correlation-ID and a Financial-Entity-ID, followed by parameters for the charge, calling and called numbers, routing numbers, the Record-Keeping server group and the calling jurisdiction information. The Billing-Correlation-ID is a 24-byte structure in the PacketCable event message specification, made of 4 bytes of NTP timestamp, 8 bytes of the unique identifier of the network element that generated it, 8 bytes giving the time zone and 4 bytes of a sequence number that increases at that element; it is encoded as a hexadecimal string of up to 48 characters, and leading zeroes may be suppressed. The Financial-Entity-ID is an 8-byte structure holding the financial identifier for the domain followed by a domain name; it is encoded as a hexadecimal string of up to 16 characters with trailing zeroes suppressed, followed by @ and the host. The accounting number parameters should all contain telephone URLs with E.164 formatted addresses.

P-DCS-LAES and P-DCS-Redirect support lawfully authorized electronic surveillance. P-DCS-LAES gives the address and port of an Electronic Surveillance Delivery Function for a duplicate stream of event messages, and may also give the address and port for delivery of call content, a billing correlation identifier of up to 48 hexadecimal digits and a call content channel identifier of up to 8 hexadecimal digits. P-DCS-Redirect carries the original destination the user asked for, the entity that performed the redirection and the number of redirections so far; for example, when A calls B, B forwards to C and C forwards to D, the Called-ID is A, the redirector URI is C and the count is 2. The RFC notes that P-DCS-Redirect overlaps in function with the History-Info header of RFC 4244, but it is continued here for backwards compatibility with existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five headers, each with one job. One carries the identity of a caller for a harassment complaint, one asks for a special kind of call handling, one carries the charging data for the call, and two carry lawful surveillance instructions. Each has a fixed syntax so that any provider's equipment can read it.

sections.title: What Each Party Does With the Headers
sections.content:
The RFC gives the rules separately for each kind of party, because what each may do with the headers differs. A trusted user agent must not include P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID in any request, because it starts the trace locally. An untrusted user agent client must insert it into the initial INVITE for a customer originated trace request, with the user information of the Request-URI set to call-trace and the host and port identifying the tracing entity. It should also include the Target-Dialog header field of RFC 4538 when it knows it, and when the remote party is unknown it should mark the user as anonymous, for example as sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid. A trusted user agent server that receives the header and finds the Request-URI set to call-trace must record and report the caller identity for law enforcement action, and then redirect the call with a 3xx response to an announcement server or to the service provider's business office. If the header is missing from such a request, the server must reject the request.

At a proxy, the trace header is removed or the request is rejected when the header appears on a request that is not a trace request. If the header carries a private-URL that identifies the proxy, the originating proxy replaces it with the verified identity of the caller of the session being traced. The proxy records the caller URL and target dialog identifiers for sessions directed at the untrusted client when the operator has provisioned it to do so, and it must reject a trace request when the URL and dialog identifier do not match a recorded incoming call. The originating proxy never adds the header to a request that did not already contain it, and a terminating proxy must not send the header to an untrusted endpoint.

For billing, the originating proxy generates the Billing-Correlation-ID and inserts the P-DCS-Billing-Info header into the initial INVITE or SUBSCRIBE, and it must remove any such header that arrived from an untrusted user agent. The terminating proxy must not send the header to an untrusted destination. Both the terminating proxy and a trusted user agent server must include a P-DCS-Billing-Info header in the first reliable 1xx (except 100) or 2xx response, carrying the correlation identifier they generated, their Financial-Entity-ID and the Record-Keeping server group. A user agent server may change the charge URI to override the billing information in the INVITE, for example for a toll-free call, but only as the service provider policy provisioned into it allows.

For surveillance the rules run the other way. The originating and terminating proxies must remove any P-DCS-LAES and P-DCS-Redirect headers in requests or responses to or from an untrusted proxy or user agent, and must not send them to an untrusted entity at all, whether as headers or attached to URIs. A proxy that is neither originating nor terminating should pass the two headers along untouched. Use of the two headers is controlled by legislation, regulation and court orders, which the RFC requires to be followed, so a SHOULD in this area means that the header must be present or must be absent depending on the applicable order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each party has a fixed job. The client that starts a trace request adds the trace header; the proxy checks it against records of earlier calls and removes it before the request leaves the trusted network; and the billing and surveillance headers are stripped whenever a message is on its way to equipment the provider does not control.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC treats quality of service gate coordination, billing information and electronic surveillance information as sensitive. All three must be protected from eavesdropping and must have integrity checking, so the trusted user agents and proxies have to take precautions against both eavesdropping and tampering.

Use of IPsec or TLS between proxies and trusted user agents is REQUIRED. A minimum mandatory-to-implement IPsec configuration for the architecture is given in the PacketCable security specification. Mutual authentication is also REQUIRED, both between proxies and between trusted user agents and proxies. It may be implemented with administratively pre-shared keys, or through consultation with another trusted third party. Where IPsec is used, the security policies and procedures of the administrative domain where the headers apply, and of every connection between administrative domains in the federation, must define an interoperable set of options.
sections.plainLanguage: The billing and surveillance data in these headers is sensitive, so the RFC requires it to be protected from being read or changed in transit. IPsec or TLS is required between proxies and trusted user agents, and the two ends must authenticate each other.

items.title: P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID
items.text: The identity of a caller, for a called party reporting a harassing or obscene call to law enforcement.

items.title: P-DCS-OSPS
items.text: A request for special call handling: busy line verification, emergency interrupt or operator ringback.

items.title: P-DCS-Billing-Info
items.text: The accounting data for a call, including the billing correlation identifier and the charging numbers.

items.title: P-DCS-LAES
items.text: Where to deliver a duplicate stream of call events, and optionally the call content, for lawful surveillance.

items.title: P-DCS-Redirect
items.text: The original destination, the party that redirected the call and the number of redirections.

viz.caption: THE OPERATOR SERVICE TAGS AND WHAT THEY ASK FOR

items.label: Busy line verification
items.desc: The user agent must send audio to the operator rather than reject the call as busy.

items.label: Emergency interrupt
items.desc: The user agent must connect the caller to the local user, who may be on another call.

items.label: Operator ringback
items.desc: The user agent must play operator ringback, such as a three-second howling tone or a sustained ring.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Defined for extensibility and reserved for future use.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE TWO SIMPLE HEADERS, AS GIVEN IN THE RFC

data.title: Header syntax
data.code:
P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID = "P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID" HCOLON name-addr
                          *1(SEMI timestamp-param) *(SEMI trace-param)
timestamp-param      = "timestamp=" 1*DIGIT ["." 1*DIGIT]
trace-param          = generic-param

P-DCS-OSPS      = "P-DCS-OSPS" HCOLON OSPS-Tag
OSPS-Tag        = "BLV" / "EI" / "RING" / token
